results.comment: 15:15 as a black man I can tell you that when this happens to me, and because of my size it happens alot, I dont even get mad anymore, I just get sad. Sad at the fact that this person took one look at me and decided I was not a human being but instead some kind of monster to be feared.     When I was younger I used to play online video games, Left for Dead 2 mostly, with this one white chick who lived in Ohio. One day, we decided to add each other on Facebook because she was planning a trip to California, where I'm at, and wanted to link up. When she saw my FB profile pic i could hear her gasp over the mic, which I thought was kinda weird since she already knew I was black. She went on to talk about how shocked she was that my voice was attached to that body and that if she ever saw me walking down the street and didn't know who I was she would be afraid for her life, day or night. She tried to make is sound like she was joking but I could tell she wasn't. Pretty much killed our friendship after that. We'll still talked for a while after that but it was never really the same. Being labeled in such a way... idk i dont think words can even describe how shitty it feels   EDIT: Since no one seems to have bothered reading my one reply.    lol.. didn't think my comment would be this popular XD. Oh, the things that happen when you turn notifications off. Setting the record straight on a few things because ppl seemed to have assumed quite a bit about my situation.  1) this shit happened 10+ years ago when I was 19. Since then I guess you can say I've  "stiffed the spine", XD and have moved on. Not married yet, but I've been with the same girl for about 7 1/2 years and going strong. Landed myself a decant tech job too so trust me when I say I'm doing good out here in these streets.   2) I'm 6'2. At the time, I was around 230 pounds so yeah a big guy but not THAT big. Not sure you some of u fucks thought I was some 400+ pound monstrosity stalking the streets of LA but I can assure you that was not the case.   3) her boyfriend at the time was around my size. From some of her FB pics I could tell we were around the same height but I, maybe, had good 30-40 pounds on him so I was definitely bigger but not to the point where I believe it would have been that shocking.   4) I've had other friends and family members experience similar situations to mine. One thing I've grown to realize over the years is that black men are seen as more of a threat than men of other races. After a while, you start to notice the way certain people react when you walk in a room or when they see you somewhere they don't expect to see a black man. The shit gets old VERY fast. Bet money the black guy in Contra's video had some incident involving a white woman in an elevator in the past and decided from now on he would do that because he didn't want any problems moving forward.    Look I get that everyone has there personal preference when it comes to dating and that's fine. Plenty of other women out there. Learning to deal with rejection is a big part of dating for men and is something I can deal with. This shit, however, this shit just felt different. I couldn't really see any other reason why she would act like that other than my race, which I still find weird since she knew I was black already.

And when he's being bombarded with TV commercials aimed at boys, that show robots and space soldier toys with an ultramasculine, deep voice in the background praising them and explosions and whatnot, while the next spot, aimed at girls, shows you princesses in pink houses while high-pitched women's voices tell you about how you can make jewellery with your (girl) friends to adorn yourself and the princess.  IMHO, toxic masculinity can not be ended by men "just stopping". Of course, that needs to happen too - grown men should become aware of these things and try to consciously work against them, just as grown women need to consciously work against the toxic ideas they have been fed. But it is as important to change how we raise children! For example, I am active in a community garden and there are also some older women and they sometimes say things that sit wrong with me. There was a boy who wanted to use the pickaxe to dig a hole and one woman said, he has to wait until men are present, implying that we women would not be able to show him how to use it. So I was like: "Don't tell the boy that nonsense - he'll believe it in the end!", took the pickaxe and went with him to show him how to use it.  Or when a group of boys on the adjacent playground excluded a girl to come onto the multi-person swing with them, while shouting: "No girls on here!" I went there, told them that excluding girls is not good behaviour. They said, "But we're swinging very heavily and she'll not like it because she's a girl." I stopped the swing, let the girl climb on and when she was settled, I said: "See, she's as capable of doing that as you:"  And when a boy was being beaten by another one, I went and tried to comfort him. (It wasn't very successful, because I think he didn't trust me enough, but I tried.)  Anyway, I try to encourage boys to be kind, but also show them it's ok to be vulnerable and ask for help. (Same for girls, of course.)  Anyway; my understanding of feminism does include uplifting men. There is such a thing as the pro-feminist men's movement. They work alongside feminists and vice versa. IMHO, feminism is only called "feminism", because anything "feminine" or associate with "feminine" is being devalued in our society. Toxic masculinity is also rooted in this. If you're vulnerable, you run a risk to be labelled as "weak" => "gay" => "like a woman". And obviously, the worst thing a man can be in our society is "like a woman". That's also while some men feel the constant need to elevate themselves above women and demonstrate to other heterosexual males, how heterosexual male they are themselves. Women can only exist as prey in such a way of thinking, not as equal partners.  So, in my understanding the first goal of feminism is, to give back value to "the feminine" (meaning things that are traditionally being considered feminine). Once it's not shameful anymore to be nurturing, non-aggressive and accommodating others (to a certain degree), etc., the next goal would be to completely dissolve the categorization into "feminine" and "masculine" for character traits. This finds its practice in encouraging men to be less aggressive and more caring, and encouraging women to be more assertive and confident. Hopefully, at one point, the genders will find themselves on equal footing without being restricted by their traditional roles.
